### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, A28, A30 and A31 (first group) and A32, A33 and A34 (second group) each ran in all 200 traces, with every first-group member before every second-group member (e.g., A28 before A32 in 100% of traces) and mixed order inside each group. In the later window, the first group appears in about 46 in 100 traces (93 of 200) and the second in about 56 in 100 (111 of 200). [OCC019, OCC020, OCC021, OCC022, OCC023, OCC024, REL013, REL015, REL025]
- The two groups became almost mutually exclusive: A28 and A32 co-occur in only about 2 in 100 later traces (100% before), with A28 running without A32 in about 45 in 100 traces and A32 without A28 in about 54 in 100; the same pattern holds for A30 and A31 against A32, A33 and A34. [REL015, REL016, REL017, REL019, REL020, REL021, REL022, REL023, REL024]
- Inside each group the members still run together: A28–A30 co-occurrence fell from 100% to about 47% (equal to the group's participation), with neither present in about 54% of later traces; A32–A33 fell from 100% to about 56%, with neither present in about 45%. [REL013, REL014, REL018, REL025, REL026, REL027]
- The connections around the groups changed: A25, which previously led only to A28, A30 and A31 (about 34%, 37% and 30% of its outgoing transitions), now also leads directly to A32, A33 and A34 (about 16–20% each); A28, A30 and A31 now lead directly to A26 in about 26–36% of their outgoing transitions, whereas A26 was previously reached only via the second group. [DIR016, DIR018, DIR020, DIR021, DIR022]
- Distances and positions moved accordingly: the gap from A25 to A32, A33 or A34 shrank from 4–5 positions to 1–3, and from A28, A30 or A31 to A26 from 4–5 positions to 1–3; the median position of A28/A30/A31 moved later (about 0.69 to 0.75) and of A32/A33/A34 earlier (about 0.78 to 0.75), so both groups now occupy the same stage; A25 itself sits slightly later within traces (mean relative position about 0.62 to 0.67) and A26 slightly earlier (about 0.83 to 0.81). [LAG004, LAG005, LAG006, LAG007, LAG013, LAG019, POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005, POS006, POS007, POS008]
- Separately, routing in the A16–A19 cluster shifted toward A17 and A19: participation fell for A16 (about 53% to 47%) and A18 (about 54% to 47%) and rose for A17 (about 48% to 54%) and A19 (about 46% to 54%); A24 now routes more to A19 (about 21% to 30%) and less to A18 (about 26% to 18%), A18 routes more to A25 (about 52% to 62%) and A19 more to A17 (about 23% to 34%). [OCC015, OCC016, OCC017, OCC018, DIR012, DIR013, DIR015]
- Smaller shifts: the A20/A27/A29 routing preferences flipped (A20 now favours A27 about 54% vs 46%, previously the reverse; A27 now favours A29 and A29 favours A21), and the A38–A42 segment became slightly busier (A38 about 1.55 to 1.70 occurrences per trace; A39 about 0.79 to 0.94, participation about 63% to 68%). [DIR014, DIR017, DIR019, OCC027, OCC028, DIR027, DIR028, DIR029]
- All remaining indicators differ only slightly (occurrence changes up to about 0.07 per trace, routing shares by a few percentage points) with empirical strengths of at most about 0.5, i.e., differences that random re-splits of stable data produce just as often. [OCC009, OCC010, OCC011, OCC012, DIR001, DIR009, DIR026]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that the stage between A25 and A26 was restructured from two sequentially mandatory groups into two alternatives: before, every case executed A28, A30 and A31 (in mixed order) and then A32, A33 and A34 (in mixed order) before A26; in the later window a case executes either the first group (about 46 in 100 cases) or the second group (about 56 in 100), with both in only about 2 in 100 — each group has become skippable, A25 now feeds directly into either group, and A26 directly follows the first group when it runs, so the second group is bypassed whenever the first executes. [OCC019, OCC022, REL013, REL015, REL025, DIR016, DIR018, DIR021]

This rests on direct relational and positional evidence rather than on frequency shifts alone: the cross-group co-occurrence collapse from 100% to about 2% with a matching only-one-group split, the preserved within-group co-occurrence, the new direct edges, the shortened lags and the converged positions all describe one consistent restructuring, and the key items exceed about 995 of 1000 random re-splits of the pooled data. [REL015, REL019, REL013, REL025, DIR016, DIR018, LAG004, LAG007, POS003, POS006, OCC019, OCC022]

Limitations: the evidence cannot show what determines which of the two groups a case takes, and it cannot fully rule out that the two windows capture different case mixes rather than a modified process; no chance-expectation baseline for the number of qualifying items is included, so the judgement rests on the directness and consistency of the relational evidence, which for this all-or-nothing pattern is hard to attribute to sampling alone. [REL015, OCC019, OCC022]

Other differences: routing inside the A16–A19 cluster moved toward A17 and A19 (with A24 rerouting accordingly), the A20/A27/A29 routing preferences flipped, and the A38–A42 segment runs slightly more often per trace; these are separate, smaller patterns and are not part of the main hypothesis. [OCC015, OCC018, DIR014, DIR015, DIR017, DIR019, OCC027, OCC028]
